walkthroughs.body_html: Born around 1162 in the harsh steppe environment, Temüjin endured the murder of his father and years of hardship before forging alliances with figures like Jamukha and Toghrul (Ong Khan). Through a mixture of charisma, ruthlessness and meritocratic promotion, he subdued rival tribes — Tatars, Keraites, Naimans and Merkits — and was proclaimed Genghis Khan (Universal Ruler) at the kurultai of 1206.

The Mongol army relied on a disciplined decimal organisation (arban, jagun, mingghan, tumen), mounted archers using composite bows, feigned retreats, psychological warfare and the use of conquered specialists (Chinese siege engineers, Persian administrators). Speed, intelligence and adaptability rather than numerical superiority underpinned their successes from Beijing to Bukhara.

By Genghis's death in 1227 the empire stretched from the Pacific to the Caspian. His sons and grandsons extended it further, producing the Pax Mongolica that allowed merchants such as Marco Polo and missionaries to traverse Eurasia. Historians debate whether the Mongols were destroyers or facilitators of cross-cultural exchange.
